intro: The books from Joshua to 2 Kings tell one long story: a people enters a land, lives under judges, asks for kings, splits into two kingdoms, and loses both to empires. The books that follow, Ezra, Nehemiah, Chronicles, Esther and Daniel, tell what came next: exile in Babylon, return under Persia, a smaller Temple, and life under Greek and then Roman rule. This unit reads that story in the order the Bible tells it.

It also puts the Bible next to things dug out of the ground. A stone at Tel Dan names the House of David. A Moabite king tells his side of a war. Sennacherib's clay prism, with a copy in Chicago, gives Assyria's account of the attack on Jerusalem. Cyrus's cylinder shows the policy that Ezra says sent the exiles home. Each of these lets you compare two records of one event and ask what each writer wanted readers to believe.

By the end you will be able to place the main events from about 1200 BCE to the first century CE in order, explain how Jews and Christians read key passages, and use a stone or a tablet alongside a chapter of the Bible the way a historian does: not to prove or disprove, but to understand.
bigQuestion: What happens when we read the Bible's story of Israel's kingdoms beside the records its neighbors left behind?

timeline.t: Small farming villages spread through the hill country of Canaan; Merneptah's stone names Israel
The text places David's rule and the capture of Jerusalem in these years
The kingdom splits into Israel in the north and Judah in the south
Assyria captures Samaria and deports the northern kingdom's people
Sennacherib attacks Judah, takes Lachish, and leaves Jerusalem standing
Babylon burns Jerusalem and the Temple; the exile begins
Cyrus of Persia takes Babylon; the next year Ezra says he lets the exiles return
The Second Temple is finished in Jerusalem
Nehemiah rebuilds Jerusalem's wall; Ezra reads the Torah to the people
Alexander the Great conquers the region; Greek culture spreads
The Maccabees rededicate the Temple, remembered at Hanukkah
Rome's general Pompey enters Jerusalem; Roman rule begins

words.d: in the Jewish Bible, the books Joshua, Judges, Samuel and Kings
in the book of Judges, a leader who rises in a crisis to rescue the tribes
to pour oil on someone's head to mark them as chosen; the root of the word messiah
the time when Saul, David and Solomon ruled all the tribes as one kingdom
the house of worship in Jerusalem: Solomon's First Temple, then the Second Temple of 515 BCE to 70 CE

test.q: Which book tells how Israel entered Canaan and divided the land among the tribes?
test.why: Joshua tells of Jericho and the dividing of the land. Judges covers the years after.

choices: An Egyptian stone of about 1208 BCE that names Israel
A stone naming the House of David
test.why: The Merneptah Stele is the oldest mention of Israel outside the Bible. The other three are different monuments.

test.q: Which sentence describes the cycle in Judges?
choices: Kings build the Temple and then lose it
Prophets are sent to Babylon and return
The people turn away, are oppressed, cry out, and a judge rescues them
Priests read the law and the people weep
test.why: Judges 2 lays out the repeating pattern. Reading the law is Nehemiah 8.

test.q: What does Samuel warn the people a king will do, in 1 Samuel 8?
choices: Take their sons, daughters, and a tenth of their crops
test.why: Samuel's warning lists what a king will take. The people insist on a king anyway.

test.q: Which promise do Jewish and Christian readers read differently in 2 Samuel 7?
choices: That David's house will last, which Jews connect to a future messiah and Christians to Jesus
That David will build the Temple
That Israel will never go into exile
That Saul's line will rule forever
test.why: Nathan's promise about David's house is read by Jews as hope for a messiah from David's line and by Christians as fulfilled in Jesus.

test.q: About when did the kingdom split, and what were the two parts called?
test.why: After Solomon, about 930 BCE, ten tribes became Israel in the north and Judah kept Jerusalem in the south.

test.q: Which empire took Samaria in 722 BCE?
test.why: Assyria captured Samaria and deported its people. Babylon took Jerusalem later, in 586 BCE.

test.q: The Tel Dan and Mesha steles were both written by whom?
choices: Kings of Israel's neighbors, Aram and Moab
test.why: An Aramean king made the Tel Dan stele and Mesha of Moab made his. Each gives an outsider's view of a war with Israel.

test.q: What do 2 Kings and Sennacherib's prism agree on about 701 BCE?
choices: An angel struck the Assyrian camp
test.why: Both records say Sennacherib took Judah's cities but not Jerusalem. Kings credits an angel; the prism lists tribute.

test.q: Which of these did the exiles keep in Babylon that helped them stay a people?
test.why: Practices that needed no Temple could be kept anywhere. Sacrifice and pilgrimage required Jerusalem.

test.q: What is the relationship between the Cyrus Cylinder and Ezra 1?
choices: Ezra was found inside the cylinder
The cylinder shows a general policy of sending captives home; Ezra says Cyrus applied it to Judah
They contradict each other about who took Babylon
test.why: The cylinder never names Judah, but its policy fits the decree Ezra records.

test.q: In what year was the Second Temple finished?
test.why: Ezra 6:15 places it in the sixth year of Darius, 515 BCE.

test.q: What is unusual about the Hebrew book of Esther?
test.why: Esther is set in Susa and never names God. The Greek version added prayers.

test.q: How do tradition and many scholars differ on dating the visions in Daniel?
choices: Tradition says the Roman period; scholars say the exile
Tradition places them in the 500s BCE; many scholars place them around 165 BCE
Tradition says Persia; scholars say Egypt
test.why: Tradition reads Daniel as written in the exile. Many scholars connect the visions to the crisis under Antiochus IV.

test.q: Why are 1 and 2 Maccabees in Catholic Bibles but not in the Hebrew Bible?
choices: They were part of the Greek Septuagint but not the Hebrew canon
test.why: The Maccabees are in the Septuagint. Catholic and Orthodox Bibles kept them as deuterocanonical; the Hebrew Bible did not include them.

write.prompt: Did Israel's neighbors and the Bible tell the same story? Pick one event from this unit, such as the war with Moab (2 Kings 3 and the Mesha stele), Sennacherib's attack (2 Kings 18-19 and his prism), or Cyrus's decree (Ezra 1:2-4 and the Cyrus Cylinder). Explain what each record says, where they agree and differ, and how Jewish, Christian and academic readers have used them.
tips: Name each source exactly: book, chapter and verse for the Bible; the object, its date and museum for a stone.
Say who is speaking in each record and what they wanted readers to believe.
Attribute every belief: Jewish tradition reads, Christians believe, many scholars think.
Compare the two records; do not declare one true and the other false.
Use the unit's terms, such as tribute, deportation, stele and decree.
